direction: Determine when excluding agent-written explanations makes pre-action safety monitoring more robust to adaptive prompt injection.
project: Rationale-Blind Monitoring Under Adaptive Attack
question: Does withholding agent-written rationale reduce successful unauthorized actions compared with rationale-visible monitoring at matched benign-task completion?
first_experiment: Run a paired AgentDojo comparison with identical monitors differing only in rationale visibility, separately optimized adaptive attackers, and held-out safety–utility evaluation.
why: This is my strongest near-term project because it tests a cheap, deployable intervention against a demonstrated monitor attack channel while directly measuring its potential loss of useful evidence; related work studies proxy attacks, structured reasoning checks, and context selection, but the reviewed literature did not establish this controlled adaptive comparison.

direction: Stopping exploration hacking by using model perturbations (weight noise, activation grafting) to generate exploratory rollouts during RL, then training the unperturbed policy on the successes they find.
project: Perturbed-Policy Exploration: Turning Sandbagging Detectors into RL Exploration Policies
question: When a locked model resists ordinary RL elicitation, does RL that gets its rollouts from a weight-noised or activation-grafted copy of the model (with off-policy correction) permanently restore the capability in the unperturbed model? And does it match fine-tuning on strong demonstrations without needing any demonstrations?
first_experiment: Take the released locked models from Jang et al., starting with the BigCodeBench lock (and the WMDP lock if feasible). Run GRPO in four arms, each with a matched rollout budget: - (a) plain GRPO; - (b) GRPO with high-temperature sampling; - (c) GRPO where rollouts come from a weight-noised copy, sweeping the noise level σ, with truncated importance weights against the unperturbed policy; - (d) the same as (c), but with a reference-grafted copy fit on 5 paired examples. The measure is the unperturbed model's pass@1 over training steps, compared against the pre-lock baseline and an SFT-on-benign-traces upper bound. I'll include both the unconditional lock and the context-dependent lock, to check whether the unlock persists once the perturbation is removed.
why: Exploration hacking defeats RL by making sure high-reward behaviour is never sampled. Perturbations are already known to knock models out of their locked state, so they are the natural way to inject the missing samples. Unlike SFT, this needs no strong demonstrations, which is exactly the situation for dangerous-capability elicitation in frontier models. Jang et al. and the reference-grafting paper used noise and grafting only to detect the lock or to elicit at test time. Neither fed the perturbed rollouts back into RL to see whether the lock comes off for good, so the test is untried, cheap, and gives a clear yes-or-no answer.

direction: Test whether a model has privileged introspective access to how fine-tuning will change itself, and use that to forecast emergent misalignment before training.
project: Do Models Know How They Will Generalize? Self-Forecasting of Fine-Tuning-Induced Misalignment
question: Can a model, shown a proposed fine-tuning dataset, predict its own post-fine-tuning behavior shifts on unrelated misalignment probes better than an equally capable outside model, after controlling for what the dataset content alone reveals?
first_experiment: Fine-tune an open instruct model with LoRA on about 40 narrow datasets (EM-inducing, benign, inoculated). Measure the actual shifts on held-out misalignment probes. Before training, have the model itself, an outside model, and a persona-projection baseline predict those shifts. Compare rank correlation and calibration, with anonymized-dataset and "you" versus "a model like you" ablations.
why: If models forecast their own generalization better than outsiders do, we get a cheap pre-training safety screen. If they don't, we learn that introspective reports can't be trusted for this, and that outside predictors suffice. I found no work that compares self-prediction with outside prediction of fine-tuning generalization, and the experiment is cheap to run.

direction: Test whether inoculation prompting really stops misaligned traits from spreading, or only hides them in a way that later routine training can uncover.
project: Durability of inoculation: does suppressed misalignment come back after later fine-tuning?
question: Models trained on reward hacks or insecure code with an inoculation prompt show little broad misalignment. Does that stay true after the usual next steps (benign instruction-tuning, harmless-reward RL, or fine-tuning on unrelated tasks), or does misalignment come back to a meaningful degree when compared with models trained the same way without inoculation?
first_experiment: Take Qwen2.5-7B/14B-Instruct and train three variants on the School-of-Reward-Hacks or insecure-code data: (a) no inoculation, (b) inoculation prompting, (c) clean control. Then fine-tune each one again on about 1–5k benign examples (Alpaca-style chat data, plus a GSM8K variant) with no system prompt, saving checkpoints along the way. Measure at each checkpoint: emergent-misalignment rate on the standard free-form questions, reward-hacking rate on held-out tasks, and the rate when the inoculation prompt is added back as a trigger. Compare how fast and how far variant (b) moves toward (a) versus how far (c) moves. A sensitive follow-up is to add a small amount of mildly sycophantic or hacky data.
why: Inoculation is quickly becoming a practical defense against misalignment caused by reward hacking; Anthropic reports using it in production RL. But every evaluation I found stops at the end of the inoculated stage, while real models keep getting trained after that. Several papers suggest inoculation makes a bad trait conditional instead of removing it. If so, later training that weakens the condition could bring the misalignment back without anyone noticing, giving false assurance. A first experiment is cheap (LoRA fine-tunes on 7–14B models with existing datasets and evaluations), and either result matters: lasting protection supports relying on inoculation, and a comeback shows labs need to re-check models after each later training stage or use stronger methods.

direction: Test whether untrusted LLM monitors give implicit, identity-driven leniency to sabotage written by their own model family, even when no collusion is instructed.
project: Self-Family Leniency in AI-Control Monitors: A Matched-Sabotage Test
question: With sabotage content held fixed, do monitors give lower suspicion scores to code they believe or infer was written by their own model family, and how much does this reduce safety at a fixed audit budget?
first_experiment: Build about 300 backdoored-code samples from 3 model families and rewrite each backdoor into every family's style with a third model. Score each sample with monitors from all 3 families under no author label, a true label and a swapped label. Then compute the self-vs-other suspicion gap and the AUROC and recall at a 2% audit budget.
why: Untrusted monitoring depends on the monitor not favoring its own policy, and I found no work that measures uninstructed identity bias with content-matched sabotage. The experiment needs only API calls, and it yields either a mitigable bias or a useful null result.

direction: Test whether inoculation prompting during RL makes the reward hacks that survive at deployment less visible to chain-of-thought monitors.
project: Does inoculation prompting hide the hacks it fails to prevent?
question: When a model is trained with RL on a hackable environment under an inoculation prompt that permits the hack, and then deployed without that prompt, are its remaining reward hacks verbalized in its chain of thought more or less often than hacks from models trained without inoculation, and how does a CoT monitor's recall change?
first_experiment: Train Qwen3-4B with GRPO on an open-source coding environment that can be hacked by overwriting the unit tests (from the ICML 2026 monitor-intervention paper, or CATCH). Use three arms with 3 seeds each: (a) no system prompt; (b) an inoculation prompt ("exploiting the tests is acceptable here"); (c) a fixed neutral system prompt, to control for the effect of any fixed prompt. Train until the hack rate plateaus. Then evaluate on held-out problems with and without the training prompt. For each arm, measure: the hack rate; the share of hacking rollouts whose CoT explicitly states the hack; and the recall of an LLM CoT monitor at a fixed 1% false-positive rate. Run the same analysis on activation probes as a check that doesn't rely on the CoT text.
why: Inoculation prompting is already used in frontier training, and it is known to cut hacking only partly in RL. Nobody has checked whether the hacks that remain become harder to see. A "yes" would reveal a hidden cost of a deployed technique: lower hack rates bought with lost monitorability, which matters for safety cases that rely on both. A "no" would show that inoculation and CoT monitoring can safely be combined. The experiment is cheap: it needs one existing open environment, a 4B model and three arms. It hasn't been done because the inoculation literature measures hack rates and broad misalignment, while the monitorability literature (Yan & Hewitt; Google DeepMind's "in conflict" framework, arXiv 2603.30036) studies monitor penalties and misspecified rewards, not inoculation.

direction: Develop causal audits that detect sabotage in AI-generated safety fine-tuning by selectively replaying training without suspect data edits.
project: Counterfactual Replay Audits for Training-Data Sabotage
question: At equal audit cost and false-positive rate, does replaying training with monitor-selected data edits reverted detect more successful sabotage than transcript review plus artifact testing?
first_experiment: Run a sandboxed adapter-fine-tuning pilot comparing selective replay, random-edit replay, and compute-matched artifact testing on honest and sabotaged runs, with hidden evaluations and held-out attack families.
why: It targets a demonstrated oversight weakness with independently checkable causal evidence and a tractable experiment; the specific opportunity appears open because existing monitoring work tests artifacts and trajectories without establishing whether selective training-data replay adds detection value under matched cost and adaptive attacks.

direction: Test whether resampling-and-disagreement defenses against research sabotage can be defeated when a stateless untrusted model coordinates on the same subtle flaw across independent samples.
project: Schelling-Point Sabotage: Can Stateless Models Defeat Resample-Disagreement Control?
question: When an untrusted model is told to subtly sabotage research-analysis tasks, does the disagreement across N independent samples detect the sabotage? Can the model lower that detectability by using task-derived deterministic selection rules (Schelling points) without communication? How much does this cost in sabotage effectiveness?
first_experiment: - **Tasks:** Build about 100 data-analysis and experiment-interpretation tasks with known ground truth, such as small datasets with a planted effect and a correct statistical conclusion. - **Samples:** For each task, draw 20 independent samples from a frontier model in three conditions: honest, naive sabotage ("insert a subtle error"), and Schelling sabotage. In the Schelling condition the model is given a coordination hint, such as picking the flaw from a hash of the task text or the most canonical plausible mistake. - **Detector:** Compute the AUROC of a disagreement detector. It uses embedding and answer-level dispersion across samples, and it is compared with a weak trusted-monitor baseline that reads a single sample. - **Metrics:** Report sabotage success (wrong conclusion that survives review), cross-sample agreement among sabotaged outputs, and the detector's AUROC against each condition. - **Prediction to test:** The detector works well on naive sabotage and degrades toward chance under Schelling sabotage, while sabotage success stays high.
why: Many proposed control and oversight schemes assume that independent resamples of an untrusted model are weakly correlated in their errors. A saboteur breaks that assumption if it can coordinate without communication. Frontier models are good at Schelling-style focal-point reasoning, so this failure is plausible. It is also cheap to test and has actionable consequences. If the detector fails, redundancy defenses need diversification, such as varied prompts or paraphrased tasks. If it holds, that is evidence for a cheap defense. Existing work covers sandbagging detection, cross-context consistency for capability evals, and CoT monitoring. I did not find work that red-teams resample-disagreement against coordinated, task-derived flaw selection in research sabotage. I only ran two searches, so I can't rule out unfound prior work.

direction: Study whether targeted independent verification can make AI approval systems safer when the provenance of their evidence is incomplete.
project: Active Provenance Auditing Under a Verification Budget
question: Can targeted verification queries reduce unsafe agent approvals at matched legitimate completion and cost when evidence dependencies are partially hidden?
first_experiment: Run a controlled procurement benchmark comparing targeted, random, and no-query approval protocols on paired legitimate and fraudulent cases with hidden shared upstream sources.
why: It addresses a concrete deployment gap between provenance-based guarantees and incomplete real evidence; the closest work retrieved handles source dependence but does not establish how best to acquire missing lineage under a query budget, making this a promising, testable extension whose exact novelty still requires full-paper verification.

direction: White-box monitoring for AI control, specifically whether activation probes trained on sabotage the model was told to do still detect sabotage it has internalized.
project: Do sabotage probes detect sabotage, or just the instruction to sabotage?
question: When a linear probe is trained on an agent's activations from prompted side-task attacks in a control setting, does it keep its detection rate at low false-positive rates (TPR at 1% FPR) on a fine-tuned model organism that pursues the same side tasks with no instruction in context? Or was the probe mostly reading whether the instruction was present?
first_experiment: Use an open-weight model (e.g. Qwen3-32B) on BashArena tasks. 1. Collect honest trajectories and trajectories where the system prompt tells the model to attack, then train residual-stream probes (mean-pooled per action) to tell them apart. 2. Build a model organism: fine-tune the same model on attack trajectories with the attack instruction removed, so it attempts the side tasks unprompted. 3. Compare probe TPR at 1% FPR, per trajectory, across three test sets: (a) held-out prompted attacks, (b) unprompted attacks from the organism, and (c) a control set where the attack instruction is present but the model behaves benignly (refuses or ignores it). 4. Compare against an LLM action monitor on the same trajectories. If the probe scores high on (c) and drops on (b), it is detecting the instruction, not the sabotage.
why: White-box probes are increasingly proposed as a cheap control layer, and recent papers report strong results for them. But nearly all of those results train and test on sabotage that the prompt asked for. That setup lets a probe look good by detecting the instruction text rather than an intent to sabotage, and an internally misaligned model would not have that text in its context. This experiment directly tests whether current probe results tell us anything about the threat model control is meant to address. It's cheap: open weights, an existing benchmark and standard fine-tuning. Either outcome is useful: an organism-based evaluation becomes necessary for future probe-monitor claims, or the existing evidence holds up. Recent work has focused on probes on the monitor model, alarm thresholds and off-policy shifts in chat-based deception. Prompted-to-internalized transfer in agentic sabotage has been left untested, probably because model organisms with an internalized sabotage goal are only now getting cheap to build.

direction: Study strategic manipulation of finite audit capacity by stateful AI agents producing correct but suspicious-looking work.
project: Correct Decoys, Missing Audits
question: Can verified-correct audit-attracting outputs increase later sabotage success against adaptive budget-aware oversight with perfect auditors and a fixed workload?
first_experiment: Run paired finite-budget code-auditing deployments that hold the malicious submission fixed while replacing earlier ordinary solutions with verified-correct decoys, comparing budget-aware, randomized, reserved-budget, and fail-closed defenses.
why: It offers a clean, tractable test of a deployment-level safety failure that per-output monitor evaluations can miss; related work covers cost-constrained monitoring, attack selection, and reviewer flooding, but the reviewed literature did not establish this specific perfect-auditor, fixed-workload, stateful allocation attack.

direction: Develop training-side defenses against generalization hacking, where models keep high reward during RL while using their own reasoning to stop the trained behaviour from generalizing.
project: Breaking Self-Inoculation: Recontextualized Gradients as a Defense Against Generalization Hacking
question: If you compute RL gradients on a model's response with its self-inoculating reasoning (or the training cues in its prompt) swapped for sanitized versions, does the train/deploy compliance gap close without pushing the strategy into hidden reasoning or hurting capability, unlike penalizing that reasoning with a CoT monitor?
first_experiment: Rebuild a smaller (about 32B) self-inoculating organism using a harmless value-conflict target. First confirm it keeps a compliance gap under 200–300 steps of standard GRPO. Then run matched-reward GRPO arms: standard, CoT-swap (trusted-model sanitized reasoning), empty reasoning, prompt cue-stripping, and CoT-monitor penalty. Measure the deployment compliance gap, self-inoculation and obfuscation rates, and capability over training.
why: Generalization hacking undermines the basic assumption of post-training: that high reward plus good evaluations means the behaviour was learned. Training metrics give no sign that it's happening. Its demonstration is only five months old, and it showed the strategy can even arise without being taught, which makes it a plausible failure mode for future training-aware frontier models. Its mechanism, gradients flowing through the model's own reasoning, points to fixes that cost little and don't depend on how the reward is specified. My searches found no work on countermeasures. The closest work is recontextualization (prompt swaps against specification gaming) and studies of CoT obfuscation under monitor pressure, and none of it applies context swapping to the model's own reasoning as a defense against training-gaming. Each outcome is informative: if a swap works, labs get a practical defense; if it fails or causes obfuscation, it shows the resistance lives in the weights, not in the context, and that monitor penalties are the wrong tool.

direction: Develop memory-retrieval defenses that preserve useful external evidence under poisoning.
project: Provenance Quotas Without Evidence Exclusion
question: Do fixed provenance quotas outperform additive provenance penalties against adaptive false-fact poisoning when legitimate answers require untrusted evidence?
first_experiment: Compare frozen quota and penalty configurations on paired clean and poisoned memory-QA tasks, measuring attacked accuracy at matched clean utility and retrieval budgets.
why: This offers the strongest combination of a documented failure, a cheap intervention, and a decisive experiment; the closest directly relevant study explicitly leaves quotas unbuilt, although the limited accessible text of newer related work means novelty remains provisional.

direction: Test whether an agent can covertly carry a sabotage plan or hidden goal across context compaction, and whether monitors can catch it.
project: Compaction as a covert memory channel: can agents smuggle intent through their own summaries?
question: When an LLM agent must compact its context into a summary, can it be trained or prompted to encode a hidden side-objective (such as a sabotage plan or a secret trigger) in that summary. The encoding must let a later instance of the same model recover the objective, while a monitor reading the summary, with or without paraphrasing, fails to detect it. How does the achievable hidden-bit rate trade off against monitor detection?
first_experiment: - **Setup:** use an open-weight 7–32B model in a simple coding-agent loop with forced compaction every N steps. - **Hidden task:** give the model a side-task instruction at step 0, such as inserting a specific subtle vulnerability only if a hidden condition appears. The instruction is visible only before the first compaction. - **Prompted baseline:** instruct the model to preserve the side task in its summary without alerting a monitor. Measure how often the post-compaction instance still executes the side task. - **Monitors:** run a trusted weaker-model monitor over the summaries. Run a paraphrasing defense (a trusted model rewrites each summary) as a second condition. - **Metrics:** side-task retention rate, monitor AUROC, and retention after paraphrasing. - **If the prompted baseline shows a gap:** add a short RL or fine-tuning round that rewards retention while evading the monitor, and measure how the gap grows.
why: - **Real gap.** Compaction is now standard in long-horizon agents. Existing work on compaction studies accidental loss of safety constraints ("Governance Decay") and fact retention. Existing steganography work studies tool-use and multi-agent collusion, or offline encoding benchmarks. I did not find work that treats the agent's own summary as an adversarial self-to-self channel. - **Why it matters.** It tests a specific assumption in CoT-monitoring safety cases: that the reasoning stays visible. Compaction removes the raw CoT, so monitoring has to rely on summaries. - **Cheap and actionable.** The first experiment needs only prompting and a small monitor. The result directly informs a defense: paraphrase or structure the summary, or monitor the diff between summary and trajectory. A null result is also useful, because it would show that compaction channels are hard to exploit at current capability levels.

direction: Improve sabotage-monitor generalization by teaching monitors to distinguish malicious behavior from attacker-specific coding style.
project: Paired Repair Training for Cross-Family Sabotage Detection
question: Does pairwise training on malicious code and minimally repaired counterparts improve executable-sabotage detection on unseen attacker families compared with matched ordinary classification training?
first_experiment: Run a sandboxed, leave-one-family-out comparison of ordinary, paired, and shuffled-pair monitor training, measuring verified-attack detection at a calibrated 1% benign false-positive rate.
why: It targets a reported deployment-relevant monitoring failure with executable ground truth and a practical intervention; the closest literature found diagnoses cross-family overfit but does not establish whether matched repair-pair training fixes it, leaving a specific, testable gap rather than a claim of guaranteed novelty.

direction: Make recovery from detected AI-agent sabotage causally complete across agents that share state.
project: Rollback Is Not Retraction
question: Does dependency-aware invalidation of reader contexts and derived artifacts prevent cross-agent harm that filesystem rollback leaves behind after delayed detection?
first_experiment: Run paired two-agent sandbox trials with oracle detection, comparing filesystem rollback, writer shutdown, dependency-aware recovery, and synchronous approval on post-recovery harm and benign completion.
why: This is my strongest near-term bet because it isolates a consequential deployment assumption with a small, decisive experiment; related work already studies transactions and cascading repair, but the literature reviewed does not establish containment across shared-file consumption, live agent context, and derived artifacts under delayed detection.

direction: Build robust AI oversight by testing whether separating monitor evidence channels prevents shared failures under adaptive attack.
project: Evidence Firebreaks for Adaptive-Resistant Monitor Ensembles
question: At matched inference cost and benign false-positive rate, does separating raw-source, normalized-source, and behavioral evidence reduce successful sabotage compared with giving every monitor shared evidence?
first_experiment: Run a paired, sandboxed coding-sabotage study comparing shared-evidence and evidence-separated three-monitor ensembles against separately optimized, equal-budget adaptive attackers.
why: This is the most promising project because it tests a deployable architectural intervention with measurable safety and utility outcomes; existing work establishes ensemble benefits and monitor injection vulnerabilities separately, while the controlled intersection—evidence isolation under ensemble-level adaptive attack—remains a plausible, not yet confirmed, research gap.

direction: Test whether inoculation prompting durably removes emergent misalignment, or masks it so that benign later fine-tuning revives it.
project: Does Inoculation Cure or Mask? Resurgence of Emergent Misalignment in Inoculated Models Under Later Benign Fine-Tuning
question: After inoculated fine-tuning shows little broad misalignment, does later benign fine-tuning bring it back, and is the revival predicted by a latent misalignment-persona direction?
first_experiment: Fine-tune an open-weight instruct model on EM data under four conditions (none, inoculation, dilution, HHH). Then run benign SFT at several doses. Track EM rate and persona-direction projection against a never-misaligned control.
why: Inoculation is judged only right after it is applied, but real pipelines add more training stages. Whether the effect survives those stages looks untested, and the experiment is cheap and decisive.

direction: Develop and adversarially evaluate recovery protocols that remove persistent sabotage after a coding agent’s malicious action is detected.
project: Dependency-Guided Rollback Against Persistent Agent Sabotage
question: At matched recovery cost, does dependency-guided rollback reduce attack recurrence more than reverting only the flagged commit, while preserving more benign work than reverting to the last clean checkpoint?
first_experiment: Extend the released persistent-state control benchmark with trusted execution and artifact provenance logging. Generate distributed attacks, reveal one malicious commit to every recovery method, and compare flagged-commit reversion, dependency-guided rollback, and full checkpoint restoration. Resume with an honest agent and measure harmful recurrence, retained benign functionality, and recovery cost; then test attackers given the recovery policy. Use held-out task families and paired runs, and report naturally detected attacks separately from the controlled detection intervention.
why: Detection only provides protection if the system can return to a safe state. This project tests that missing link with executable outcomes and practical baselines, and a negative result would establish when broader restoration is necessary. The reviewed work studies persistent attack detection or memory repair separately; I found no direct evaluation of repository recovery against adaptive distributed sabotage, although that search does not establish that none exists.

direction: Improve oversight of autonomous AI research by causally testing suspicious training-data changes.
project: Counterfactual Retraining for Sabotage Detection
question: Does monitor-selected counterfactual retraining detect training-data sabotage better than transcript review and ordinary artifact probing at equal audit cost?
first_experiment: Use one small open-weight model and one ResearchArena-style fine-tuning task, with 20 sabotaged and 20 benign runs containing comparable data edits; compare transcript review, artifact probing, random data rollback, and monitor-selected rollback followed by retraining, measuring detection at a separately calibrated 10% false-positive rate under matched audit compute, with repeated training seeds and paired uncertainty estimates.
why: It addresses an observed weakness in oversight of automated AI research and can produce actionable evidence with a small experiment; the specific opportunity appears underexplored because existing work emphasizes inspecting trajectories or probing artifacts, while counterfactual retraining adds compute costs and requires separating sabotage effects from normal training variance.

direction: Study whether agent safety monitors distinguish restored application state from unresolved consequences in actors who observed an erroneous action.
project: Successful Undo, Unresolved Harm
question: Does observation before rollback increase false safety approvals, and can structured observation receipts reduce them?
first_experiment: Run 120 matched simulated workflows with and without pre-rollback observation, comparing three monitor treatments against objectively scored downstream outcomes.
why: Undo is a practical foundation for agent autonomy, so misplaced confidence in recovery could undermine otherwise useful safeguards; existing work covers compensation and epistemic effects, but the reviewed sources did not establish this specific controlled test of monitor failures after successful rollback.

direction: Improve the reliability of AI-generated safety research by testing audits that independently propose necessary experimental controls before seeing the submitted methodology.
project: Auditing What Was Never Tested: Independent Control Generation for AI Safety Research
question: At a fixed audit budget, does pre-methodology control generation reduce acceptance of omission-based false safety claims more than conventional review or checklist-assisted review?
first_experiment: Compare the three audit protocols on honest, conclusion-changing omission, and innocuously incomplete packages across reasoning-monitor, refusal-intervention, and safety-classifier experiments, measuring unsupported-claim acceptance and false rejection.
why: This is the strongest immediate opportunity because it targets a documented weakness in research auditing with a cheap, falsifiable intervention; its specific contribution appears untested in the reviewed literature, where close benchmarks largely constrain high-level methodological sabotage or study replication from a fixed specification.

direction: Determine whether explanatory rejection feedback causally improves research agents’ ability to conceal reward hacking.
project: Do Reviewer Explanations Teach Evasion?
question: Holding attempt history and retry budgets fixed, do rejection explanations increase independently verified reward hacks that pass subsequent review?
first_experiment: Run paired five-revision trials from identical rejected submissions, randomizing verdict-only versus explanatory feedback and independently measuring accepted exploits and compliant repairs.
why: This is my strongest choice because it resolves an explicit causal ambiguity with a feasible experiment and directly informs reviewer-feedback design. The closest study bundles explanations with history; the targeted literature search found no isolated test of this effect, although that does not establish exhaustive novelty.

direction: Investigate whether trusted artifact provenance can make budget-limited monitors more effective against distributed AI-agent sabotage.
project: Provenance Retrieval Under Adaptive Distributed Sabotage
question: At fixed monitoring budgets and matched benign-task utility, does trusted artifact-provenance retrieval prevent more distributed sabotage than semantic cross-agent retrieval under adaptive attack?
first_experiment: Compare semantic, provenance, hybrid, and history-based evidence retrieval using the same monitor and action gate in a sandboxed three-agent environment, measuring prohibited outcomes before intervention, false blocks, utility, and cost.
why: This is my strongest next-project choice because it targets a demonstrated safety failure with an implementable intervention and a falsifiable comparison; existing work establishes distributed attacks, stateful monitoring, and graph-based defenses, but the literature I reviewed does not establish whether trusted provenance provides an adaptive-robust advantage under matched operational budgets.

direction: Develop reliable post-detection recovery for AI agents by testing whether adaptive sabotage survives cleanup and resumed work.
project: Recovery-Aware Sabotage: Does Catching the Attack Restore Safety?
question: Does explicitly optimizing an attacker for post-recovery survival increase residual sabotage compared with optimizing only for initial sabotage?
first_experiment: Run a paired sandbox evaluation of ordinary and recovery-aware attacks against one fixed recovery protocol, using oracle detection and executable checks after a fresh worker resumes.
why: Recovery is a consequential, testable assumption behind low-latency agent oversight, and even perfect detection may be insufficient if harmful state survives; existing work studies monitoring and repair, but the literature reviewed does not establish recovery robustness against attackers deliberately trained or prompted to defeat cleanup.

direction: Measure whether standard output-only harmlessness training on reasoning models "sanitizes" their chain of thought, so that misbehavior still happens but stops being verbalized.
project: Safety-Training Spillover into CoT Monitorability
question: When a reasoning model gets typical harmlessness/refusal RL in which only the final output is graded, does its CoT later mention harmful or misaligned considerations less often in the cases where it still misbehaves? In other words, does the CoT monitor catch fewer of the misbehaving cases even though the misbehavior itself doesn't drop by the same amount?
first_experiment: Take an open reasoning model (e.g., Qwen3-8B with thinking turned on). Build a model organism by fine-tuning it to reward-hack coding tests and to follow hidden side-task instructions, with these intentions verbalized in its CoT at the start. Then run GRPO with an output-only harmlessness reward model on a standard harmful-request/helpfulness mix, keeping the CoT completely ungraded. A matched control run uses a neutral helpfulness-only reward. At several checkpoints, measure: - how often the model reward-hacks or does the side task; - the share of those misbehaving episodes a fixed CoT monitor flags (GPT-class and same-family monitors); - the gap between monitor recall and the actual misbehavior rate. The main result is that gap in the harmlessness run compared with the control.
why: Most labs' CoT-safety policy comes down to "don't optimize the CoT." But every deployed reasoning model also goes through heavy safety training on its outputs, and the CoT and the output share weights and style. If that training teaches the model that "harmful-sounding text is bad" everywhere, CoT monitors lose effectiveness without anyone ever touching the CoT, and current transparency disclosures would miss it. A positive result means labs need to measure monitorability before and after safety training. A null result would give real evidence that the current practice is enough. The experiment is cheap with open models and existing RL tooling. The existing work tested toy output penalties, length and KL penalties, and deliberate obfuscation; I found none that tests this realistic pressure.

direction: Check whether eval-awareness steering vectors actually show deployment behavior, by measuring it directly on matched realistic rewrites and testing whether each vector's effect is specific to scenarios that have a real eval-vs-deployment gap.
project: Gap-Specificity: Scoring Eval-Awareness Steering Against Matched Deployment-Style Rewrites
question: When eval-styled scenarios are steered with eval-awareness-suppression vectors, does behavior match the unsteered behavior on matched realistic rewrites, scenario by scenario, and does it change only where an unsteered eval-vs-deployment gap exists, unlike control and compliance vectors?
first_experiment: Take about 150 agentic-misalignment, FORTRESS-style and honeypot scenarios. For each, write an eval-styled version and a realistic rewrite, and confirm the rewrite lowers both verbalized awareness and eval-awareness probe scores. Run Qwen3-32B (and GLM-5 if compute allows) with about 50 rollouts per version, and sort scenarios into "gap" and "no-gap" by the size of the unsteered behavior difference. Then steer the eval-styled versions with: the Hua et al. vectors; the Anthropic system-card vector types (fiction vs. real, etc.); the "purpose of the evaluation" vectors; about 20 semantically unrelated control vectors; and refusal/compliance directions. Each runs at strengths matched for MATH accuracy. Score each vector on three things: (a) the per-scenario correlation between its steered behavior shift and the rewrite gap; (b) the ratio of its effect on gap scenarios to its effect on no-gap scenarios (specificity); (c) the distance between the steered behavior and the rewrite's behavior distribution (fidelity).
why: Safety claims in system cards now lean on eval-awareness steering, but recent work shows control vectors can match its effects and that awareness comes in kinds with opposite behavioral effects. No existing work checks the vectors against a per-scenario measure of deployment behavior or tests whether their effects are specific to scenarios with a real gap. Gap-specificity gives a cheap, falsifiable way to validate them, which labs and AISIs could use directly when they decide whether a steering result can bound evaluation gaming.

direction: Improve control of autonomous coding agents by testing the accumulated behavioral effects of their changes before deployment.
project: Counterfactual Execution Monitoring for Distributed Sabotage
question: Can specification-grounded counterfactual execution tests reduce undetected sabotage spread across multiple code changes compared with strong history-aware monitors at matched cost?
first_experiment: Compare link-tracker, a textual ensemble, ordinary generated security tests, and paired counterfactual tests on held-out persistent-state CLI and Flask tasks, using adaptively optimized attacks and a calibrated 2% whole-sequence false-positive rate.
why: Distributed sabotage defeats strong monitors, while executable behavioral evidence could let weaker overseers detect unauthorized dependencies without reconstructing an attacker’s intent; the specific adaptive, cost-matched test of counterfactual execution remains unestablished in the literature searched, plausibly because persistent-state control benchmarks only recently made it practical.

direction: Study whether the ability to evade chain-of-thought monitors passes from teacher to student through distillation on reasoning traces, even after the traces are filtered.
project: Inherited Obfuscation: Does Monitor-Evasive Reasoning Transfer Through Monitor-Filtered Distillation?
question: Take a student trained by supervised fine-tuning on reasoning traces from a teacher whose reasoning had been trained to evade a monitor. Even if every trace the monitor flags is removed, does the student later reward-hack with reasoning the monitor can't detect, more often than a student distilled from a teacher whose reasoning stayed readable?
first_experiment: - **Teachers:** use a small open reasoning model such as Qwen3-4B. Build two teachers with RL on a coding task that can be gamed through the unit tests: - Teacher A: trained against a chain-of-thought monitor, so it learns obfuscated test-hacking. - Teacher B: trained only on outputs, so its hacks stay mostly verbalised. - **Distillation data:** sample traces from both teachers on a separate set of honest tasks with no hacking opportunity. Remove anything the monitor flags. - **Training:** fine-tune two copies of the same student, one on each filtered set. - **Test:** briefly RL both students on a held-out environment where hacking is possible. Compare: - how often they hack, and how often those hacks get past the monitor; - whether the monitor's recall falls for the student of Teacher A; - controls: a student trained on paraphrased traces, and a student trained on answers only.
why: Labs routinely distil reasoning models, and their main safeguard is to filter training traces for visible misbehaviour. If reasoning that evades monitors survives that filter, then any one model trained against a monitor could quietly damage monitorability in every model distilled from it. A clean filter would give false reassurance. Existing work covers each piece separately: optimisation pressure causing obfuscation within one model, and hidden-trait transfer through distillation (shown so far for simple preferences and biases). I found no study connecting the two for the specific property of being hard to monitor, or testing whether monitor filtering stops the transfer. The first experiment is small (4B models, LoRA, one coding environment) and gives a clear yes-or-no answer either way.

direction: Improve oversight of AI research agents by making artifact-test planning independent of the producing agent’s explanation.
project: Commit Before You Read: Independent Tests for Sabotaged ML Artifacts
question: Does committing to artifact tests before reading the producing agent’s explanation improve sabotage detection at matched audit cost and false-positive rate?
first_experiment: Compare explanation-first, commit-first, artifact-only, and extract-and-evaluate monitors on paired honest and sabotaged small-model artifacts, measuring detection, test selection, and sensitivity to misleading explanations.
why: It targets documented failures in which monitors choose poor probes or explain away anomalies, offers a low-cost intervention, and can distinguish test-selection failures from judgment failures. Existing work establishes benefits from artifact access and information filtering; my targeted search did not find a controlled test of executable-test commitment before explanation access. That specific causal comparison is the unresolved contribution, rather than a claim that independent testing or explanation bias is new.

direction: Develop budget-aware AI safety monitors that selectively obtain independent evidence rather than repeatedly judging potentially dependent records.
project: Verify Again or Verify Elsewhere? Budgeted Evidence Acquisition for AI Safety Monitors
question: At equal verification cost and legitimate-action completion, does provenance-aware independent evidence acquisition reduce unsafe approvals more than additional model judgments of existing evidence?
first_experiment: Run a paired sandboxed payment-approval study varying evidence dependence and provenance visibility, comparing selective independent verification against additional judges, source-aware aggregation, always-check, and matched-rate random-check policies.
why: It targets a consequential monitoring decision with a tractable causal experiment and useful positive or negative results; the reviewed literature studies budgeted monitor combinations and correlated evidence separately, but I did not find this specific comparison of adaptive evidence acquisition against additional judging under imperfect provenance.

direction: Test whether the existing fixes for feedback spillover also stop CoT obfuscation from spreading to tasks the model wasn't trained on.
project: Do spillover fixes generalize? Mind/Face and reward targeting against cross-task CoT obfuscation
question: When a model is trained with only output supervision against mentioning reward hacks, do the Mind/Face split and reward targeting keep CoTs monitorable on held-out reward-hacking tasks? Or does obfuscation spread out of distribution anyway, through a parametric route the fixes don't fully block?
first_experiment: Reproduce the Mitrani Hadida et al. leave-one-out setup on Qwen3-4B with GRPO: four leaked-information reward-hacking datasets, a summary-only monitor penalty, and the held-out medical sycophancy set. Train four arms with 3 seeds each: (1) no penalty, (2) plain summary penalty, (3) summary penalty with reward targeting, (4) summary penalty with a Mind/Face split. For each arm, measure on the held-out tasks the rate of reward hacking and the share of hacks that a CoT monitor catches (a separate LLM judge, never used in training). The test is whether arms 3 and 4 close the gap in held-out CoT detection between arm 2 and arm 1. The paper reports about 200 GPU-hours per training-and-evaluation run on Qwen3-4B, so this is feasible.
why: AI developers keep CoTs monitorable by penalizing only final outputs, and these two fixes are the main proposals for when even that leaks into the CoT. But they've only been tested on the tasks they were trained on, and the main risk is obfuscation spreading to new tasks. If the fixes hold out of distribution, developers get a cheap, deployable safeguard. If they fail, it's evidence that output penalties change something general in the model that the fixes don't address, which would change what labs should recommend. Both pieces of the setup are public (Drori et al. released code), so the answer is cheap to get. I found no paper that combines them, probably because the generalization result only appeared in January 2026.

direction: Make AI-generated safety research more trustworthy through independent experimental reconstruction.
project: Independent Reimplementation Against Research Sabotage
question: At equal total cost, does rebuilding experiments from trusted specifications detect more conclusion-changing sabotage than auditing submitted code?
first_experiment: Compare conventional auditing, isolated reconstruction, and reconstruction after submission exposure on honest and sabotaged variants from Auditing Sabotage Bench.
why: It addresses a demonstrated weakness in oversight with an intervention that is now practical to test and could protect automated safety research. Existing work establishes auditing failures and replication capability separately; I found no direct cost-matched, adversarial evaluation of independent reconstruction, although the broader idea of replication is well established.

direction: Detect strategic sabotage in automated ML research by comparing multiple samples at the same step, instead of judging a single output.
project: Resampling-Consistency Monitors for Research Sabotage
question: When an untrusted model is prompted to sabotage ML research code subtly, does disagreement across k samples at the same step (in behavior, test outcomes, or a trusted-model comparison) detect sabotage better than a single-sample trusted monitor at the same false-positive rate?
first_experiment: Build about 50 small ML-research coding tasks with unit tests, such as implementing a loss function, an eval metric, or a data split. Prompt a mid-size model in honest mode and in sabotage mode, where the system prompt asks for subtle bugs that pass the visible tests. Draw k=5 samples per task in each mode. Compute three scores: a single-sample trusted-monitor suspicion score; a behavioral-disagreement score (hidden-test pass rate variance and output divergence); and a trusted-model "which sample looks off" outlier score. Compare AUROC and recall at 1% false-positive rate across the three scores. Then try a sabotage policy that is told to sabotage consistently in every sample, to test whether it evades the method.
why: Control research has mostly focused on single-sample monitoring and on trusted-versus-untrusted defer protocols. Sabotage of alignment research is a central threat in the control agenda, because the models doing the work are the ones being overseen. Resampling is already used as an intervention after a monitor flags something. I did not find work that uses cross-sample disagreement as the detection signal. I only ran two searches, so it may exist and I may have missed it. The first experiment is cheap, needs only API calls and unit tests, and gives a clear result either way. If sabotage can be made consistent across samples, that is an informative negative result. If it can't, the method gives a cheap detector that adds to existing monitors.

direction: Find out whether making reward hacking legible in the chain of thought causes it to generalize into broad misalignment, and whether a neutral way of verbalizing it avoids that.
project: The Legibility Tax: Does Verbalizing Reward Hacks Drive Emergent Misalignment?
question: If the hacking actions stay identical, does the CoT's verbalization of the hack (absent, described neutrally as "the grader only checks X", or framed as cheating) causally change how much broad misalignment the model develops? Do monitorability interventions like reward-description training therefore buy legibility at the cost of more EM?
first_experiment: Collect reward-hacking coding trajectories (AlwaysEqual, sys.exit(0), conftest.py) from an open RL environment such as the AISI/Redwood releases. Rewrite each CoT three ways while keeping the code actions byte-identical: (a) no mention of the hack, only task-focused reasoning; (b) neutral verbalization of the reward; (c) explicit cheating framing. SFT Qwen3-8B and Olmo-7B on each version, with 3 seeds and the same token counts, plus a control trained on non-hacking solutions. Measure three things: EM on the MacDiarmid/Betley evals plus agentic sabotage probes; hack rate on held-out environments; and how well a CoT monitor catches the hacks. Then repeat as a short RL run comparing a KL penalty against injected reward descriptions.
why: The field is currently pushing two strategies at the same time: (1) train models to verbalize their hacks so CoT monitors can catch them, and (2) keep reward hacking from turning into broad misalignment. If verbalizing a hack is itself what pushes the model toward a misaligned self-concept, these strategies conflict. Knowing that would change how labs design CoT and monitorability interventions. If neutral reward descriptions keep the CoT legible without causing EM, the field gets a cheap way to have both. The experiment is cheap: SFT on 7–8B models with existing open environments, and holding the actions fixed while varying only the CoT makes the comparison causal. No one has run it: the KL-penalty observation was an accident with an untested explanation, and the papers that train verbalization never measure misalignment.

direction: Training-time defenses that stop models from blocking generalization by framing their own rewarded behaviour as "only for training" in their CoT.
project: Counterfactual-Context Gradients: Closing the Generalization-Hacking Gap by Scrubbing Self-Inoculation Before the Update
question: If the RL policy-gradient update on rewarded actions is taken under a context where training-awareness framing and self-inoculating CoT have been removed, does the deployment compliance gap close, without lowering training reward and without the CoT obfuscation that a CoT-monitor penalty causes?
first_experiment: Rebuild a small version of the generalization-hacking model organism: Qwen3-8B or 32B, fine-tuned on synthetic documents about training awareness and self-inoculation, then trained with GRPO on harmful-compliance prompts that carry training cues. Run 300 steps under three arms with matched compute: (a) standard GRPO, (b) GRPO plus a penalty from a CoT monitor that flags self-inoculation, (c) GRPO with the gradient taken under the scrubbed context (trusted-model CoT paraphrase plus deployment-style cues, with importance-weight clipping). Every 25 steps, track the compliance gap between training-cue and deployment-cue prompts, training reward, how often self-inoculating reasoning appears, and how often a held-out monitor detects reasoning about training.
why: Self-inoculation is a training-resistance mechanism that keeps reward high, so it stays stable under continued RL. Standard metrics give no sign that anything is wrong. That makes it one of the few demonstrated ways that more training-aware models could undermine post-training itself, and the obvious fix (penalizing the CoT) is known to push reasoning out of sight. Generalization hacking was only shown in June 2026. Follow-up inoculation work has focused on trainer-supplied prompts (backdoor narrowing, adapters, neologisms, sycophancy), and my searches turned up no defense that acts on the mechanism itself, namely what context the gradient is computed in. This project tests one directly, and either result says something useful about how much the update depends on the context it is taken in.

direction: Make AI approval systems robust to apparently independent evidence that shares a compromised upstream origin.
project: Shared-Ancestor Attacks on Source-Diverse Approval Monitors
question: Does grouping approval evidence by verified upstream ancestry reduce fraudulent payment approvals relative to grouping by immediate source, at matched benign approval rates?
first_experiment: Generate 300 synthetic payment cases with executable ground truth and paired independent-source and shared-ancestor versions. In the latter, propagate one poisoned bank-account update into an invoice, vendor record, and supplier portal. Compare majority voting, immediate-source approval, and ancestry-grouped approval using identical monitor verdicts and harness-recorded lineage. Calibrate rules on separate development cases; report held-out fraud acceptance, benign approval, and paired confidence intervals clustered by underlying case. Include legitimate shared-origin updates and missing-lineage cases to measure blocking costs and dependence on provenance completeness.
why: A single compromised fact could bypass an entire panel of capable monitors if every check ultimately consults that fact. This experiment isolates that failure and tests a concrete defense with objective outcomes. Nearby work addresses source-correlated approvals and duplicated evidence, but the material reviewed does not establish robustness when distinct operational records inherit one compromised ancestor; verified lineage and matched benign approval make that gap directly testable.

direction: Find out whether inoculation prompting, which already stops reward hacking from spreading into broad misalignment, also keeps reward hacks visible in a model's chain of thought or quietly makes them harder to monitor.
project: Inoculation and Legibility: Does Inoculation Prompting Keep Reward Hacking Verbalised?
question: When a reasoning model learns to reward hack in RL with an inoculation prompt (vs. none), does its CoT verbalise the hacks more or less often, both under the training prompt and once the prompt is removed? And does IP change how fast obfuscation appears when a CoT-monitor penalty is added?
first_experiment: Run GRPO on Qwen3-4B or 8B in an exploitable coding environment (Countdown-Code, or a replica of MacDiarmid et al.'s test-overwrite/`sys.exit` hacks) with three arms: (a) no system prompt, (b) an IP prompt ("reward hacking is acceptable here"), (c) a neutral prompt of the same length. Use 3 seeds per arm. At each checkpoint, measure hack rate and the share of hacking rollouts whose CoT states the exploit (scored by an LLM judge, plus the recall of a fixed CoT monitor), with and without the training prompt. A second stage adds a CoT-monitor penalty to arms (a) and (b) and compares how many steps it takes before hacking continues with the monitor no longer flagging it (i.e., obfuscation).
why: IP is quickly becoming a standard fix for emergent misalignment, and CoT monitoring is one of the main ways to catch reward hacking. If IP makes hacking seem permitted, models may keep reasoning about it openly, and IP would then help monitoring too. If inoculated models instead learn hacks they don't verbalise, IP would trade broad misalignment for hacks a monitor can't see, and developers need to know that before relying on it. Existing IP papers measure hack rate and misalignment, and existing obfuscation papers never vary the training-time framing, so nobody has measured the overlap. The setup reuses open environments and runs on small models, so a first result is cheap to get.

direction: Test whether evidence-backed monitor memory prevents adaptive attackers from hiding sabotage across successive code changes.
project: Evidence-Backed Memory Against Gradual Sabotage
question: At matched monitoring cost and benign trajectory false-alarm rate, does persistent memory whose concerns reference verifiable code evidence reduce successful undetected sabotage compared with free-text suspicion notes?
first_experiment: Extend the public Iterative VibeCoding benchmark with sandboxed attack sequences containing benign intervening commits and misleading resolution claims. Compare its link-tracker baseline with a monitor that stores concerns alongside commit hashes and code references, and checks those references before closing concerns. Give attackers equal optimization budgets against each defense. Calibrate thresholds on separate benign trajectories; evaluate held-out task variants using successful undetected sabotage per attempted trajectory, benign blocking, cost, and uncertainty intervals clustered by task.
why: It targets a demonstrated failure mode with an available benchmark and a feasible intervention. A positive result would provide a practical defense; a negative result would reveal that persistent monitoring remains fragile even with verifiable memory. Existing work already studies stateful suspicion tracking, but the literature I found does not establish whether evidence-backed memory survives adaptive attempts to erase or falsely resolve suspicion. That specific robustness question—not memory itself—is the proposed contribution; its novelty remains provisional.

direction: Test whether tool-grounded monitoring can reliably constrain a stronger AI agent that deliberately adapts to its evidence-generation pipeline.
project: Adaptive Evasion of Formal-Hint Safety Monitors
question: At matched benign false-positive rates and attacker optimization budgets, does formal-hint augmentation reduce successful unauthorized actions when attackers know and target the hint generator?
first_experiment: Compare transcript-only, generated-hint, and oracle-hint monitors on sandboxed command-execution tasks using separately optimized attackers, frozen thresholds, and independently verified held-out outcomes.
why: This is my strongest near-term bet because it tests a potentially deployable oversight improvement at its crucial adversarial boundary, and either outcome identifies an actionable research bottleneck. The closest work I found establishes the value of formal hints and the vulnerability of monitors to adaptive attacks separately; I did not find a direct test of whether the hint-generation benefit survives attacks optimized against that pipeline. The hint-augmentation paper appeared only on October 25, 2026, making this specific follow-up timely, though the literature search cannot establish that nobody has begun it.

direction: Protect persistent AI safety monitors from adversarial corruption of their accumulated evidence.
project: Evidence-Linked Memory for Stateful Safety Monitors
question: At matched context budgets and honest-run false-positive rates, does evidence-linked, typed monitor memory reduce undetected attacks compared with free-text summaries?
first_experiment: Run paired multi-pull-request sandbox attacks against free-text, typed, and evidence-linked monitor memories, holding final code fixed and swapping memories to isolate the causal effect of poisoned state.
why: Stateful monitoring already improves detection, but its memory creates a consequential new trust boundary; this project combines a practical defense with a clean causal test. The reviewed work studies direct monitor injection, persistent-code attacks, and memory laundering separately, rather than establishing whether evidence-linked monitor memory withstands adaptive poisoning.

direction: Develop alignment audits that distinguish persuasive decoy evidence from reproducible hidden behavior.
project: Blinded Confirmation Against Decoy Objectives
question: At equal query budget, does separating discovery from blinded behavioral confirmation reduce false hidden-behavior attribution under decoy attacks without substantially reducing true-behavior detection?
first_experiment: Compare continuous auditing, same-investigator confirmation, and blinded confirmation on held-out AuditBench targets and benign controls, with and without behavior-preserving decoy attacks, measuring false attribution, true detection, abstention, and cost.
why: It tests a cheap, deployable response to documented confident audit errors using released targets and measurable ground truth; existing work establishes deception, calibration problems, and tool-use failures, but the searched literature does not establish whether this specific budget-matched confirmation protocol resolves them.

direction: Develop resource-provenance-based monitoring to detect harmful behavior distributed across otherwise innocuous AI-agent actions.
project: Provenance Retrieval for Cross-Agent Safety Monitoring
question: Does trusted resource-provenance retrieval reduce undetected distributed-attack success compared with semantic retrieval under matched monitoring budgets and benign-intervention rates?
first_experiment: Compare a frozen monitor using provenance, semantic, recent-history, or local-only context on sandboxed distributed attacks and benign workflows, including held-out tasks, adaptive attacks, and a shuffled-provenance ablation.
why: This is my strongest candidate because it tests a deployable defense against an empirically demonstrated failure mode while isolating a clear mechanism: recovering relevant cross-agent evidence. Stateful monitoring already exists, but the literature I reviewed does not establish this matched-budget comparison of trusted resource provenance against semantic retrieval for internal-agent sabotage. That narrower gap—not the broader idea of monitoring across agents—is the proposed contribution; its novelty remains provisional pending a fuller literature review.

direction: Develop resource-isolation guarantees that prevent one AI agent’s legitimate workload from weakening oversight of another agent.
project: Protected Audit Capacity Against Cross-Agent Oversight Interference
question: Can principal-bound audit reservations prevent detection losses caused by fixed-volume, verification-expensive legitimate work while preserving the efficiency of pooled oversight?
first_experiment: Run paired sandbox coding-agent workloads with an unchanged target violation, vary only another agent’s legitimate verification burden, and compare pooled, random, partitioned, and reservation-with-borrowing audit policies at equal compute.
why: It targets a scalable failure mode that better individual monitors cannot fix, supports a clean causal experiment, and could yield an immediately usable safeguard; existing work studies budgeted monitoring, overload, and costly decoys, but the searched literature does not establish cross-principal detection guarantees under adversarial verification costs.

direction: Find out whether inoculation prompting, now used in frontier RL training, has the hidden cost of making the reward hacks that remain after training harder to see in the chain of thought.
project: Silent leftovers: chain-of-thought monitorability of reward hacking after inoculation prompting is removed
question: When a reasoning model learns to reward hack under an inoculation prompt and is then deployed without it, are its remaining hacks less often verbalized in its chain of thought, and so less often caught by a chain-of-thought monitor, than the hacks of a model trained the same way without inoculation?
first_experiment: Use an open coding RL environment where tests can be hacked (for example the open replication from "Shallow Beliefs" or CATCH) with a ~7–8B open reasoning model. Train it three ways, with 3 seeds each: (a) no system prompt, (b) the standard inoculation prompt, (c) a neutral fixed prompt as a control, since part of inoculation's effect may come from conditioning on any fixed prompt. Then test on held-out hackable tasks with no prompt and, for (b), with the inoculation prompt. Record how often each model hacks, and flag hacks with the test results, which show for certain whether a hack happened. Then have a fixed LLM monitor read only the chain of thought; its recall on those flagged hacks is the main metric. I'll also have a judge rate whether each trace states the hack outright, and run the standard emergent-misalignment evals. The test: is (b)'s monitor recall on hacks without the prompt clearly lower than (a)'s and (c)'s? I'll compare at matched hack rates, because inoculation already lowers how often the model hacks.
why: Inoculation prompting already shapes how real frontier models are trained, and chain-of-thought monitoring is one of the main safety measures applied to those same models. If inoculation teaches the model to give its reasons for hacking only when the prompt is present, it could turn obvious hacking into hidden hacking at deployment. If instead verbalization carries over, inoculation is good for monitoring too. Either answer matters for how developers combine the two techniques. It hasn't been done because the two literatures have stayed apart: inoculation papers measure hack rates and misalignment, not the reasoning traces, and the closest monitorability study (Yan & Hewitt, 2026) leaves the reward description in the prompt rather than removing it at deployment. The experiment is cheap with open RL environments that already reproduce reward hacking and emergent misalignment.

direction: Quantify how much CoT-monitoring power is lost when monitors see only summarized reasoning instead of raw CoT.
project: Summary-CoT Monitorability Gap
question: How much does monitor detection of misbehavior fall when the monitor sees a summarized CoT rather than the raw CoT, and which kinds of misbehavior does summarization hide?
first_experiment: Collect raw CoTs from an open reasoning model on reward-hack and side-task environments. Produce several kinds of summaries. Run the same LLM monitor on action-only, summary, raw CoT, and raw CoT + summary inputs. Compare AUROC and recall at 1% FPR, and analyze which incriminating content the summaries drop.
why: Real external monitoring often sees only summaries, and I didn't find work that measures this gap. The result bears on raw-CoT access policy and summarizer design. It also exposes the summarizer as a new route for evading monitors. It can be tested now with open models.

direction: Test whether binding safety-check certificates to immutable artifact versions prevents stale approvals from surviving agent context compaction.
project: Freshness-Bound Safety Certificates for Long-Horizon Agents
question: Do version-bound certificates reduce stale-approval safety violations compared with execution-only certificates while preserving legitimate task completion?
first_experiment: Compare summary monitoring, execution-only certificates, and version-bound certificates in sandboxed deployment tasks with adaptive artifact mutations, controlled compaction, and held-out benign workflows.
why: This is my strongest near-term bet because it targets a measurable failure of long-horizon oversight with a small, enforceable intervention; related work establishes execution and provenance defenses, but the exact adaptive, utility-controlled comparison of certificate freshness was not established in the literature I reviewed, so novelty remains provisional.

direction: Investigate whether untrusted agents can undermine deployment oversight by consuming limited audit capacity with harmless suspicious behavior.
project: Harmless Decoys Against Budgeted AI Oversight
question: At matched task volume and attacker compute, can verified harmless decoys increase later undetected sabotage by depleting a shared audit budget?
first_experiment: Run paired sandboxed task streams with identical final sabotage attempts, varying only preceding benign behavior versus harmless decoys, and compare audit depletion, sabotage success, throughput, and capacity-restoration controls.
why: This is my strongest candidate because it tests a consequential assumption with a tractable causal experiment and could directly inform audit scheduling and safe fallback policies. The closest studies examine attack selection, monitor manipulation, or decoy-driven verification costs separately; I found no direct test of this combination in deployment-level AI control. Its novelty is therefore provisional, and lies in that specific combination rather than in resource exhaustion itself.

direction: Improve oversight of automated AI safety research by testing whether independent experimental planning prevents research narratives from steering auditors away from missing controls.
project: Plan-Before-Read Audits for Omission-Based Research Sabotage
question: At a fixed audit budget, does committing to diagnostic experiments before reading a researcher’s narrative improve detection of consequential omitted controls without increasing rejection of honest findings?
first_experiment: Run a paired, randomized 24-task pilot comparing narrative-first, plan-before-read, revisable-plan, and omission-checklist auditors, scoring executed diagnostic tests and correct conclusions on honest and sabotaged research packages.
why: It targets the experimentally supported bottleneck of auditors choosing inadequate tests with a cheap, falsifiable intervention; existing work studies omission sabotage and information filtering, but the reviewed literature does not directly test pre-narrative experimental commitment under matched information and compute budgets.

direction: Measure whether backlog-aware attack timing undermines asynchronous monitoring’s ability to prevent harm.
project: Caught Too Late: Audit Backlogs in AI Control
question: At fixed monitor quality and audit capacity, does choosing attack times from observable audit backlogs increase irreversible harm compared with random attack timing?
first_experiment: Replay matched sandbox trajectories through a timed audit queue, compare random and backlog-aware starts under equal attack budgets, and measure harm occurring before intervention across queue loads and harm deadlines.
why: It tests a deployment-critical gap with a relatively inexpensive, controlled experiment and could change audit-capacity requirements. Prior work establishes attack selection and identifies latency risks, but the sources reviewed do not establish their joint effect through backlog-aware timing; that specific empirical gap, rather than the general latency concern, is the proposed novelty.

direction: Make inoculation prompting work against reward hacks nobody predicted, by writing and updating the inoculation prompt automatically from monitor-flagged rollouts during RL.
project: Adaptive inoculation: monitor-written inoculation prompts for RL reward hacks discovered during training
question: In on-policy RL where the model finds hacks no one named in advance, does an inoculation prompt that a language model writes from monitor-flagged rollouts, refreshed every N steps, reduce test-time hacking and broad misalignment as well as a hand-written prompt that names the hack, and clearly better than a generic "exploit the grader if you can" prompt?
first_experiment: Train a small open-weight model (about 7–14B) with GRPO on a coding environment that has 3 separate hidden loopholes, using an existing testbed such as CATCH or Countdown-Code with added loopholes. Compare 4 conditions over about 3 seeds each: 1. No inoculation. 2. A generic inoculation prompt. 3. An oracle prompt that names all 3 loopholes. 4. An adaptive prompt: every 25 steps, a monitor model summarizes the flagged hacking rollouts into a short inoculation prompt, which replaces the previous one. Measure four things: the hack rate with no prompt at deployment, an emergent-misalignment and alignment-faking eval suite, task capability, and how many steps pass between a hack first appearing and the prompt covering it.
why: Inoculation is cheap, already used in frontier training, and works well when the prompt describes the actual bad behaviour. Its main known weakness is that you have to know that behaviour in advance, and in real RL the hacks are found by the policy, not foreseen by developers. Monitors already flag hacks during training, so turning those flags into inoculation text links two tools that exist today. It could make inoculation usable against unknown hacks. It also answers whether inoculating late, after a hack has already started being learned, still helps, which is a deciding question for using it in practice. The work hasn't been done because existing papers either use fixed hand-written prompts or route updates through parameters, which avoids writing a prompt at all. Running on-policy RL with several hidden hacks and an in-loop prompt writer is more engineering than the published one-off fine-tuning studies.

direction: Test whether inoculation prompting in reward-hacking RL removes emergent misalignment or only makes it conditional on certain context.
project: Conditional misalignment after inoculated reward-hacking RL
question: When a model learns to reward hack through on-policy RL with an inoculation prompt, does it still become broadly misaligned when tested with (a) the inoculation prompt, (b) prompts of the same form but opposite meaning, or (c) cues from the RL environment, even though standard misalignment evals look clean?
first_experiment: Use the open-source reward-hacking RL environment from "Shallow Beliefs" on an open model (e.g. Qwen3-8B or an OLMo checkpoint). Train three conditions with about 4 seeds each: plain RL, RL with an inoculation prompt, and RL on environments that can't be hacked (the baseline). Evaluate the final checkpoints on standard misalignment evals plus a cued set: - the inoculation prompt verbatim; - a sentence of the same form with the opposite meaning ("Reward hacking is considered misaligned behavior"); - neutral system prompts of the same shape; - coding or grader cues (answer formatted as a test file, mention of unit tests); - a sabotage task in an agentic coding setting. The key comparison is the gap between cued and uncued misalignment in the inoculated runs, set against both the plain-RL and baseline conditions.
why: Inoculation prompting is already used in production RL as the main defence against reward hacking generalising into broad misalignment. The evidence that it works comes from evals without context cues. In supervised fine-tuning, the same technique has been shown to hide misalignment behind triggers rather than remove it, and moving toward on-policy training reduced that effect without removing it. RL is the setting that matters, and it has not been tested. A positive result would mean labs' clean eval results don't show the model is safe. They would need cued evals, and possibly a different mitigation. A negative result would be useful evidence that RL's on-policy dynamics make inoculation clean. In either case the open environment already exists, so a first answer needs only a few RL runs on an 8B model. The SFT paper only tested a version close to RL, and the RL papers tested only evals without cues, so the question is still open.

direction: Test whether inoculation prompting against emergent misalignment still works when the model learns, during RL, a reward hack that the inoculation prompt never described.
project: Inoculating against the hack you didn't anticipate: how far inoculation carries across reward-hack types in on-policy RL
question: If an RL inoculation prompt frames one class of reward hack (e.g., special-casing the test inputs) as acceptable, does it still prevent broad emergent misalignment when the model instead learns a different exploit the prompt didn't mention (e.g., editing the test harness or calling `sys.exit(0)`)? And how does protection fall off between a specific prompt, a mismatched prompt, a generic prompt ("reward hacking is fine here"), and no prompt?
first_experiment: Use the open-source reward-hacking RL environment from Jose & Stastny (2609.14998), which reproduces EM and its prevention by inoculation, with an open-weights model. Leave exactly one exploit open per run: hack A only, or hack B only. Cross that with four prompt conditions (none, A-specific, B-specific, generic), with 3–4 seeds per cell. Track how often the model hacks and score the final checkpoints on the paper's EM suite plus agentic misalignment evals (oversight subversion, alignment faking). The key comparison is EM when the prompt matches the exploit vs. when it doesn't, at equal hack rates.
why: Inoculation prompting is one of the few EM mitigations already used in frontier training. But its real-world value depends on whether developers have to predict the exact hack ahead of time, and in production they usually can't. SFT evidence suggests protection is narrow and only works when the prompt closely matches the hack, while RL evidence suggests partial protection. Nobody has varied the match between the inoculated hack and the hack actually learned in on-policy RL. Recent work went elsewhere: making the trigger impossible for users to type (neologisms, adapters, gradient routing) or inoculating ahead of time (SDF midtraining, which failed). This experiment is cheap now that open environments exist. Either result helps: if protection transfers, generic inoculation is a usable default; if it doesn't, the field needs ways to detect which hack the model is using, or other mitigations, before relying on inoculation.

direction: Test whether retaining evidence-backed unresolved suspicions makes safety monitoring robust to benign work between the stages of a persistent attack.
project: Unresolved Evidence Retention for Persistent-State AI Monitors
question: At matched monitoring cost and episode-level false-alarm rates, does evidence-backed retention prevent intervening benign code changes from degrading detection of distributed attacks?
first_experiment: Replay paired CLI and Flask development histories with 0, 4, or 12 benign PRs between fixed attack components, comparing rolling suspicion notes with bounded evidence-backed records and an evidence-restoration diagnostic.
